questions.q: Which grape, the larger-berried sibling of Petit Manseng, leads the dry white the Court lists as Jurançon Blanc Sec?
questions.exp: Jurançon is made from Gros Manseng and Petit Manseng: the higher-yielding Gros Manseng leads the dry Jurançon Sec, while thick-skinned Petit Manseng, left to shrivel on the vine late into the autumn, gives the sweeter plain Jurançon, which the Court calls off-dry. The Court lists the two Mansengs as the Southwest's white grapes.

questions.q: Madiran AOP is Tannat-dominant. Which partner grapes does the Court list beside it?
questions.exp: The Court lists Madiran as Tannat with Cabernet Franc and Cabernet Sauvignon, and Cahors as Côt (Malbec) with Merlot and Tannat; both appellations make dry red wine only. Their firm tannin is why the Court pairs them with duck breast, rack of lamb, foie gras, cassoulet and Périgord truffles.

questions.q: Domaine Tempier, Château de Pibarnon and Château Pradeaux are the Court's named producers for which Provence appellation?
questions.exp: All three are Bandol estates: Tempier built the appellation's name on Mourvèdre, Pibarnon farms high limestone terraces at La Cadière-d'Azur, and Pradeaux at Saint-Cyr-sur-Mer makes reds of almost pure Mourvèdre. Bandol red must be at least half Mourvèdre and spend eighteen months in wood, and the Court pairs it with beef and lamb.

questions.q: The Court names Domaine du Mas Blanc and Chapoutier as producers to know for which appellation?
questions.exp: Domaine du Mas Blanc at Banyuls-sur-Mer and the Rhône house of Chapoutier are the Court's Banyuls producers. Banyuls and Banyuls Grand Cru are Grenache vins doux naturels from the schist terraces above the sea at the Spanish border; Maury is the neighbouring Grenache vin doux naturel of the upper Agly, Fitou a dry red of the Languedoc and Bandol a Provence red.

questions.q: Which style dominates the output of Côtes de Provence AOP, as the Court describes it?
questions.exp: Côtes de Provence is rosé-dominant, pale and dry, from Grenache, Cinsault, Syrah and Mourvèdre, and the Court gives Provence as a whole nearly 90 per cent dry rosé. Rolle, the Vermentino of Italy, leads its small output of white; Bandol, by contrast, is dominated by red.

questions.q: The Court pairs Provence dry rosé with shellfish, fish and one Marseille fish stew above all. Name the stew.
questions.exp: Bouillabaisse, rockfish simmered with saffron, fennel and orange peel and served with rouille, meets a cold, dry Provence rosé or a white Cassis, whose acidity and herbs match the broth. The Court's other southern pairings are Banyuls with chocolate, figs and blue cheese, Cahors and Madiran with duck and cassoulet, and Monbazillac with fruit desserts and foie gras.

questions.q: Still red Limoux AOP is led by which grape, by the Court's account?
questions.exp: Limoux lies high in the upper Aude valley, cooler and touched by the Atlantic, so its red is Merlot-dominant where most Languedoc reds rest on Grenache, Carignan and Syrah. Its dry whites come from Mauzac, Chenin Blanc and Chardonnay, and Crémant de Limoux adds Pinot Noir for white and rosé traditional method sparkling wine.

questions.q: Which river rises in the Massif Central and flows west through the vineyards of Bergerac and Monbazillac?
questions.exp: The Dordogne flows west past Bergerac, south-east of Bordeaux's Right Bank, then on past Libourne to meet the Garonne in the Gironde. Bergerac makes dry whites, reds and rosés from the Bordeaux grapes, and Monbazillac, on the river's left bank facing the town, makes botrytised sweet white from Sémillon, Sauvignon Blanc and Muscadelle.

questions.q: By the Court's account, Provence, the birthplace of wine in France, has made wine since about when?
questions.exp: Greek settlers founded Massalia, now Marseille, around 600 BC and planted the first vines in what became France, which is why the Court calls Provence the birthplace of French wine. The Court dates grape growing in the Southwest from 125 BC, under Roman rule.
